pārameśvaraṃ kimapi kṛtyaṃ nirvāhaṇīyamiti so'saṃbhavannapi saṃbhāvya eva | prayatna iti caturvidhasya kṛtyasya tatprāṇitatvāt | tatprasādādeva iti yatraiva parameśvarātmā prasanno dehādyabhimānakāluṣyatyāgena, sa eva mohamahārṇavāduttarītuṃ samarthaḥ | tat iti parameśvarokte śāstre yā upapāditā bhāvena iti saṃskāro dīkṣādikriyā dhyānādiyogo yogo jñānaṃ tasyāḥ samantataḥ sāmarthyāt tāṃ tām iti heyarūpāṃ dehaprāṇapuryaṣṭakaśūnyādipramātṛmayīṃ bhogādhārabhogyādilakṣaṇāṃ bhuvanabhāvādimayīṃ bhuvaṃ pariharaṃstyajan svayaṃ dhyānayogajñānādiṣu parameśvaraguruprasādadvāreṇa ca dīkṣādau sa parameśānugṛhītaḥ prakāśatāṃ nayati aiśvaryamātmani,-iti pūrveṇa (page 168) saṃbandhaḥ | iyati dīkṣādīnāṃ sarveṣāṃ sāmarthyamuktaṃ yadatraiva janmani parameśvaratālābha iti yogajñānayoḥ prādhānye'pi jñānadīkṣāpūrvakatvāt | yadāgamo na cādhikāritā dīkṣāṃ vinā yoge'sti śāṅkare | kriyājñānavibhedena sāca dvedhā nigadyate || (mā. vi. 4|6) iti | yadātu dhyānayogānanabhyasyanneva jñānadīkṣāsamāśvastastadā asya kimityāha bhāvanā iti | kecit iti yoginaḥ | vibhūtibhāgam iti sarvajñatvasarvakartṛtvayoraṃśamadhikajñānakaraṇasāmarthyamaṇimā- divibhūtyaṣṭakalakṣaṇaṃ tattadbhuvanaviśeṣaviṣayamiti | tadanena pratyakṣata eva adhikasadbhāve'pi na prakṛtasya hāniriti pradarśya yuktyā api etadeva upapadyate ityāha nahi iti | ātmabhāva iti paramātmana iti ca | ubhayatrāpi parasparaṃ sannidhānayorna virodha iti uktam | nanu mā bhūt prāṇāderātmabhāvasannidhānena paramātmanaḥ sannidhāne virodhaḥ, svasaṃvedanātmakasvaprakāśatvavirodhastu bhavet | maivam, saṃnihitaścet paramātmā, tadasau svaprakāśaikasvabhāvaḥ | tadāha naca iti | nanu paramātmā cet svaprakāśaḥ, tarhi prāṇāderātmabhāvaḥ katham | tatprathā iti paramātmano yā svātantryeṇa prathā, tatprabhāvādeva tasya iti prāṇādeḥ tathā iti ātmatayā prakāśanaṃ yataḥ | etadeva draḍhayati apareṣāmapi iti prāṇādervedakatāspṛktvamasti vedyatāyāmapīti ekagrahaṇam | bhāvānām iti vastūnām | etat spaṣṭayati avastūnāmapyevam iti darśa
**Grace, initiation, and the one liberated while living** All that has been established — the valid means, its fruit, the primacy of the knower — now comes to its practical point. How does one actually attain the Lord? The whole vimarśa closes with the answer: by the Lord's grace, working through a fourfold effort, and culminating in the one liberated while still living. There is a supreme work to be accomplished. Even if it seems impossible in itself, it is undertaken as possible; and the effort that drives it is the life of the fourfold work. But the decisive factor is not the effort alone — it is the *grace* of the Lord. Only when the Lord's self is pleased, when the turbidity of our conceit in the body and the rest is abandoned, are we able to cross the great ocean of delusion. The means are laid out in the Lord-taught teaching: the initiatory rite (dīkṣā), the vision-yoga (dhyāna), knowledge (jñāna), and devotion (bhāvanā). By their combined capacity, the aspirant abandons the world that is to be left behind — the knower-made world of body, breath, the eight-fold city and the void, the world of the things that support and objectify enjoyment — and, through the grace of the Lord and the guru, brings the lordship itself to manifestation within his own self. The order matters. Although vision and knowledge are primary, knowledge is preceded by initiation. As the teaching says, there is no eligibility for the yoga of Śaṅkara without the dīkṣā; and the dīkṣā is twofold, by rite and by knowledge. But what if one, assured by the knowledge-initiation alone, has not practiced the vision-yoga? Then there is devotion (bhāvanā). Some, the yogins, attain a share of the wondrous powers — a portion of all-knowing and all-doing, the eight-fold vibhūti, pertaining to this or that world. But even where such powers are manifest, nothing of the present goal is lost; and this, too, is established by reason. Now a subtle point about the self. The prāṇa — the vital breath, the body, the rest — is experienced as "I." How is this compatible with the param-ātman, the supreme self? There is no conflict, because the two are present together. The prāṇa's being felt as "I" is nothing other than the supreme self's own free manifestation: the param-ātman shines freely, and by that very shining the prāṇa and the rest appear as "I." Even the knower-ness that touches them is that same light. The object is remembered, because experience is broken and re-collected; but the knower — whose essence is the un-broken light — is not something that could be remembered. As the Spandakārikā says, remembered-ness is not how the essence is realized. So the Lord-ness is not a new thing to be proved in the consciousness-essence; and the negation of "I" in the breath and the body is not a new discovery either. Both were there from the beginning. And so the end. In all this there is the utter extinction of the delusion-impression. And when that is extinguished, when the restraint of the body-and-"I" conceit dissolves, there is the Lord-ness itself. Yet even here, by the Lord's will alone, for some the recognition does not arise despite a hundred efforts. But even for such a one, merely by coming to hear the teaching, by the ordered ripening of the impression, there is necessarily the attainment of one's own form. The āgama declares: "Unwavering in self-experience, he is called the jīvanmukta, the one liberated while living; but he who still constructs the essence — at the fall of the body, he goes to Śiva." And Abhinavagupta adds his own verse: the sparks of the pure-knowledge-fire blaze when the inner intent is ended, like the root-leaves of the old tree of saṃsāra caught in the fire of the supreme reality. Hence, by all this, **nothing new is established in the self**. The Lord was always the own self; grace, initiation, vision, knowledge and devotion only reveal what was already there. This, Abhinavagupta says, is what was declared at the very beginning of the tea
